young.html: What does everyone want most? Aristotle says: to be happy. But he doesn't mean feeling cheerful for an afternoon. He means a whole life that goes well, which the Greeks called eudaimonia. A happy life, he says, comes from being a good person and doing good things, over a long time. One sunny day doesn't make a summer, and one good day doesn't make a happy life.

How do you become good? By practice, the way you learn anything. You become a builder by building and a musician by playing. In the same way, you become fair by doing fair things, and brave by doing brave things. Good habits become part of who you are.

Aristotle's most famous idea is the golden mean. A good habit sits between two bad ones: one with too little, and one with too much. Courage is between being a coward (too little) and being reckless (too much). Being generous is between being stingy and being wasteful.

young.name: gb-golden-mean
young.cap: Pick an area of life and slide from too little to too much. Then try “The mean for you.”

young.html: Find the middle. Make three cards for each of these: “Too little,” “Just right” and “Too much.” Act out a situation (a friend asks to borrow your favorite toy; you see a big spider; someone tells a joke you don't like). Others hold up the card that fits your reaction. What would “just right” look like?
Aristotle also says that good friends are one of the greatest treasures in life. The best friends, he says, like each other for who they are, not just for what they get from each other.

full.html: The Nicomachean Ethics, from Aristotle's last years of teaching in Athens (about 335–322 BC), is named for his son Nicomachus, who may have edited it. It is part of what Aristotle calls the study of politics: how people should live, alone and together. He warns at the start that ethics cannot be as exact as mathematics, and that it is for people who already have some experience of life.

Everything we do aims at some good, and most goods are wanted for the sake of others: we want money for what it buys. There must be a final good, wanted for itself. Everyone calls it happiness (eudaimonia, flourishing), but people disagree about what it is: pleasure, honor or wealth. Aristotle argues from what is distinctive about human beings, our reason. Happiness is activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, over a complete life, with enough friends, health and goods to live it.
There are virtues of thought, learned by teaching, and virtues of character, learned by habit:

full.text: We learn an art by doing that which we wish to do when we have learned it; we become builders by building, and harpers by harping. And so by doing just acts we become just, and by doing acts of temperance and courage we become temperate and courageous.
full.author: Aristotle

full.html: A virtue of character concerns feelings and actions, which can go wrong by excess or by defect. Virtue aims at the mean, but not an arithmetic middle:

full.text: But the mean relatively to us cannot be found in this way. If ten pounds of food is too much for a given man to eat, and two pounds too little, it does not follow that the trainer will order him six pounds: for that also may perhaps be too much for the man in question, or too little; too little for Milo, too much for the beginner.
full.author: Aristotle
full.note: Milo of Croton was a famous wrestler.

full.name: gb-golden-mean
full.cap: Each virtue between two vices. The mean is not always the exact middle, and it depends on the person and the situation.

full.text: Virtue, then, is a habit or trained faculty of choice, the characteristic of which lies in observing the mean relatively to the persons concerned, and which is guided by reason, i.e. by the judgment of the prudent man.
full.author: Aristotle

full.cap: Some of Aristotle's virtues and vices, in our own words (Books II–IV).

full.title: The mean is not the middle
full.q: If ten pounds of food is too much and two too little, what is the arithmetic middle? Why might a good trainer not order it?
steps: But the right amount depends on the person: a champion wrestler like Milo needs more, a beginner less.
So the mean “relative to us” is found by judgment of the case, not by arithmetic.
full.a: 6 pounds is the middle of the numbers, but the right amount depends on the person

full.html: Thinking the mean means always being moderate or lukewarm. Sometimes great anger, or great generosity, is exactly right. And some actions, like theft, have no mean at all: they are wrong in any amount, Aristotle says.

items: Choice and responsibility (III): we are praised or blamed for what we do willingly; actions done under force or through ignorance of the facts can be excused.
Justice (V): giving shares in proportion to what people are due, and setting right losses in trade and wrongs.
Practical wisdom (VI): phronēsis, the skill of seeing what is right in a particular case, ties all the virtues together.
Weakness of will (VII): against Socrates, Aristotle grants that people can know the better and do the worse, overcome by desire.

full.html: Aristotle gives friendship two whole books. There are three kinds: friendships of use (business partners), of pleasure (people who have fun together), and of character, between good people who wish each other well for each other's own sake. The first two end when the use or the fun ends. The third is rare, takes time, and lasts. A good person, he says, relates to a friend as to himself, “for his friend is another self.”

The highest happiness, Aristotle concludes, is a life of contemplation, thinking about the highest things, because it is the activity of our best part and the most self-sufficient. The life of practical virtue, in family and city, is happy in a second way. The book ends by turning to laws and education, the subject of the Politics.

deep.html: Aristotle's Ethics is the founding book of what is now called virtue ethics, which asks “what kind of person should I be?” rather than only “what rule should I follow?” Medieval readers, Thomas Aquinas especially (later on this ladder), joined Aristotle's virtues with the Christian virtues of faith, hope and love. In the 1700s and 1800s, Kant (duty) and Mill (the greatest happiness), also on this ladder, built ethics on rules and consequences. In the twentieth century, philosophers such as Elizabeth Anscombe and Alasdair MacIntyre argued for returning to Aristotle's approach.

Psychologists today study habits, character strengths and what makes people flourish, and some cite Aristotle. Critics ask whether the mean gives enough guidance, and note that Aristotle's list of virtues fits the life of a free male citizen of his time.

items: Is happiness a feeling, or a way of living?
Can you become brave by acting brave, even when you don't feel brave?
Do you have a friend of the third kind? How did that friendship grow?

questions: What makes a whole life happy, not just a day? Ask the oldest person you know.
What is a good habit you have built by practice? How long did it take?
Think of a time someone was too brave, or not brave enough. What would the middle have looked like?
Which of your friendships are for fun, which are useful, and which are for who the person is? Can one friendship be all three?
Aristotle says the right amount depends on the person. Can you think of an example in your family?
Is it possible to know what is right and still not do it? What helps?
